$description: The Arabic side of the type system. It is a separate file rather than more entries in typography.json because the Latin values were authored as one set of decisions and these are a second set answering the same questions for a script with different metrics — keeping them apart makes it visible when one side has moved and the other has not. Every token here has a Latin counterpart and none of them is a concept only Arabic has, which is why script is a mode of this scale rather than a parallel scale beside it (see content/rules/rtl-arabic.md §2 and decision 007). Nothing here is a fork: if a rule below turns out to be true of Latin as well, it belongs in typography.json instead. letter-spacing is deliberately absent from this file and there is nothing to add to it. Arabic script is cursive and joined, so non-zero tracking severs the joins and a word stops being a word — the existing letter-spacing.none in typography.json is the only permitted value for Arabic text and no Arabic tracking token exists to be reached for. The audit found the failure this prevents: a global letter-spacing: 0.01em inherited by every Arabic product title in Market, while two Move components had already fixed it locally for Latin reasons. That is a rule settled inside a component, which is the thing this file and the rule layer exist to make unnecessary.

font-family.$description: The Arabic stack. Its counterpart is font-family.sans, which is Latin-only: a Latin-only stack does not fail loudly on Arabic text, it silently delegates the rendering to whatever face each operating system picks as a fallback, so the same string is set in a different face on iOS, Android and Windows and nobody chose any of them. That is the specific gap this token closes, and closing it is a precondition for the optical correction below, which cannot be calibrated against 'whatever the OS picked'.

arabic.$description: A named face first, real Arabic system faces behind it, a generic last. IBM Plex Sans Arabic leads because it is drawn to sit against Plex Latin at matched proportions, which turns the Arabic/Latin optical relationship into something measurable rather than something each designer estimates, and because it carries regular, medium and semibold as real weights — the three that font-weight declares — so none of them is synthesised. Synthesised bold is worse in Arabic than in Latin: smearing a glyph thickens the joins between letters as much as the letters, and the word closes up. The chain behind it is not decoration. It renders while a webfont is still arriving and when it never arrives at all, and every entry in it is a genuine Arabic face — Apple's SF Arabic, Segoe UI on Windows, Noto Naskh Arabic on Android, ChromeOS and Linux, then the older Geeza Pro and Tahoma — so a failed download degrades to correct-but-different rather than to broken. system-ui is deliberately not in this stack: it is not an Arabic face, it is a promise that the OS will choose one, and that promise is the defect being fixed. The open tension worth naming: font-family.sans is deliberately download-free, and this stack leads with a face that is not. Arabic is where the inconsistency actually costs something, and Plex Sans Arabic is openly licensed so the cost is bytes rather than money — but if Mizan later commits to a licensed Latin face that is not Plex, this first entry is revisited rather than kept out of habit.

figma-token-sync.specimen.note: What to set this stack in when something renders it as a specimen rather than reading its value. It lives here because the tool that draws the specimen is brand-agnostic machinery and may not hold a line of Arabic — it can prove that a variable is bound, but only this file can say what the face is supposed to be doing. Without it the Figma proof sheet bound this stack to a text node reading font-family/arabic, which is Latin: an Arabic face was shown setting characters it does not have, the operating system quietly substituted another face for them, and the swatch looked correct. That is the one failure the proof sheet exists to make visible, so a specimen that cannot fail is worse than no specimen. The string is the opening of the classic Arabic pangram — 'describe the form of a maiden like the sun' — chosen over a plain label for three reasons that are all about what it exercises. It joins: every word carries initial, medial and final forms, so a face that breaks the cursive connections shows it in the first word. It is voweled: the sukoon and kasra marks sit above and below the line, which is the exact interference the arabic line-height steps in this file were set to clear, so the specimen and the leading tokens are demonstrating the same claim. And it is conventional: an Arabic typographer recognises it as a specimen line rather than reading it as product copy, which a translated UI phrase invites. Not a translation of anything and not user-facing — nothing ships this string; changing it changes what the proof sheet says and nothing else.

line-height.$description: Three steps, one for each Latin step, same names with an arabic- prefix and different values — the shape of the two scales is identical on purpose, because a mode has nothing to resolve if the two sides have different numbers of rungs. Arabic needs more leading at the same size: ascenders and descenders reach further than in Latin, and diacritics sit above and below the line rather than inside it, so consecutive lines interfere at ratios Latin tolerates comfortably. typography.json set the Latin ratios generously so that Arabic inheriting them would not be actively broken; these replace 'not broken' with 'correct'. The size of the gap is the evidence for why one value cannot serve both: Arabic body text needs roughly what Latin uses for long-form passages, so the two scales are offset by about a full step rather than by a rounding error, and any single shared value is either cramped Arabic or loose Latin.

arabic-tight.$description: The counterpart of line-height.tight (1.25), for headings and short single-line text. Still the tightest step, and still not for anything that wraps past about two lines. The correction here is the smallest of the three because tight text is one or two lines, so the collisions this scale is guarding against arise less often — but it is not zero, because a single Arabic heading that wraps once puts a final descender directly under the tooth of the line below, which is the collision Latin at 1.25 does not produce.

arabic-normal.$description: The counterpart of line-height.normal (1.5), and the default for body text. The largest correction of the three lands here deliberately: this is the step almost all text uses, and it is the one place where multi-line running text and diacritics occur together, which is where the two scripts diverge most. 1.75 is where Naskh at the base size stops feeling compressed without the lines starting to drift apart from each other.

arabic-relaxed.$description: The counterpart of line-height.relaxed (1.7), for long-form passages and for the smallest sizes where extra leading is what keeps lines from interfering. The correction is smaller than at normal because the Latin value is already generous, so less is needed to reach adequacy. This is also the ceiling: above roughly 1.9 a paragraph stops reading as a block and starts reading as a list of separate lines, which is a worse failure than being slightly tight.

font-size.$description: One correction, not a second eight-step scale. A parallel Arabic size scale would be eight more values to keep in step with eight Latin ones, and the two would drift the first time somebody adjusted one end; a single multiplier cannot drift because there is only one of it. This group carries no $type so that its member can declare its own — the value here is a ratio, not a dimension, and typing it as a dimension would invite somebody to write px into it.

arabic-scale.$description: The optical correction applied to any font-size step when the text is Arabic. Arabic and Latin at the same nominal font-size do not appear to be the same size — the em box is spent differently, and Arabic set at a Latin size reads as the smaller of the two, which is why the rule layer has always called optical matching a decision rather than an accident. Expressing it once as a token is the point: the alternative is every designer nudging a size by eye and no two of them landing in the same place. The value is not chosen freely. It is capped by the type scale's own tightest step: font-size.100 to font-size.200 is 12px to 13px, a ratio of 1.083, so a correction of 1.083 or more would push the Arabic rendering of one rung onto the Latin rendering of the next and collapse an eight-step scale to seven. 1.08 sits just under that ceiling, which is also the honest reason it is not the 1.10 or 1.12 that some Arabic/Latin pairings want — the scale cannot absorb more, and if a larger correction is ever needed the 12/13 pair has to be reconsidered first. Because line-height is expressed as a unitless ratio, the correction propagates into leading for free and must not be applied to line-height a second time. Applied as a multiplication on the size, not with CSS font-size-adjust: that property normalises on x-height, and Arabic has no x-height to normalise on.
